level1.text: The weather satellite NOAA-20 orbits the Earth in a nearly circular orbit of radius $7196\,\text{km}$. The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$. Calculate the orbital speed of the satellite. Give the answer in kilometres per second.
A GPS satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit of radius $26\,560\,\text{km}$ at the speed $3.87\,\text{km/s}$. How long is the orbital period of the satellite? Give the answer in hours.

A geostationary communications satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit of radius $42\,164\,\text{km}$. The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$. Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the satellite.

The Moon orbits the Earth in a nearly circular orbit of radius $384\,400\,\text{km}$, and its orbital period is $27.3\,\text{d}$. Calculate the orbital speed of the Moon. Give the answer in kilometres per second.

A probe orbiting the Moon follows a circular orbit of radius $1847\,\text{km}$. The mass of the Moon is $7.35 \cdot 10^{22}\,\text{kg}$. Calculate the orbital speed of the probe. Give the answer in kilometres per second.
An astronaut floats on a space station that orbits the Earth at an altitude of $400\,\text{km}$. Which of the following explains the floating?
level1.answer: The astronaut and the station are in free fall with the same acceleration, so there is no normal force.

choices.text: Earth's gravity at an altitude of $400\,\text{km}$ is so weak that hardly any force acts on the astronaut.
choices.feedback: Gravity has not weakened much: the distance from the centre of the Earth grows by only about $6\,\%$, so the gravitational force is still about $88\,\%$ of its value at the surface. The astronaut floats even though the force acts.

choices.text: The gravitational force and the centrifugal force pulling the station outwards are equal and cancel each other.
choices.feedback: The forces do not cancel each other. Only the gravitational force acts on the satellite, and it is the net force of the circular motion, which turns the direction of the velocity towards the Earth. If the net force were zero, the body would continue in a straight line.

choices.text: The astronaut and the station are in free fall with the same acceleration, so there is no normal force.
choices.feedback: Correct: both the station and the astronaut move under gravity alone with the same acceleration. The station does not push the astronaut anywhere, so the normal force is zero and the astronaut is weightless even though the gravitational force acts on him or her.

choices.text: The station moves so fast that its speed keeps the astronaut in the air and gravity does not act on him or her.
choices.feedback: Gravity acts on the astronaut all the time. A high speed does not cancel gravity but prevents falling to the Earth: the body falls towards the Earth, but because of the sideways speed the surface of the Earth curves away from under it.

level1.text: Jupiter's moon Io orbits Jupiter in a nearly circular orbit of radius $4.22 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km}$. The mass of Jupiter is $1.90 \cdot 10^{27}\,\text{kg}$. Calculate the orbital speed of Io. Give the answer in kilometres per second.

The Earth orbits the Sun in a nearly circular orbit of radius $1.496 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{km}$ and orbital period $365.25\,\text{d}$. Calculate the orbital speed of the Earth. Give the answer in kilometres per second.

Phobos, a moon of Mars, goes round Mars in an almost circular orbit of radius $9380\,\text{km}$. The mass of Mars is $6.42 \cdot 10^{23}\,\text{kg}$. What is the order of magnitude of the orbital period of Phobos according to the circular-orbit model?

choices.feedback: Here the square root has been forgotten: $\tfrac{\gamma M}{r}$ is the square of the orbital speed, $v^2$, not the speed $v$. The speed would come out about $4600\,\text{km/s}$, so the period becomes far too short.

Here the radius has been put under the square root in kilometres but into the circumference $2\pi r$ in metres. The speed then comes out $\sqrt{1000} \approx 32$ times too large and the period equally too short.
Correct: the orbital speed is $v \approx 2.1\,\text{km/s}$, and the period $T = \tfrac{2\pi r}{v} \approx 2.8 \cdot 10^{4}\,\text{s}$ is about $7.7\,\text{h}$.
Here seconds have been converted to hours by dividing by $60$. Dividing by $60$ gives minutes; an hour has $3600\,\text{s}$, so the result is $60$ times too large.

level1.text: The left side of the figure shows the Earth's orbit round the Sun. Read from the figure the Earth's smallest and largest distance from the Sun and use their mean as the radius of a circular orbit. The mass of the Sun is $1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\,\text{kg}$. How large is the Earth's acceleration in the circular-orbit model? Give the answer in the unit $\text{mm/s}^2$.

A probe orbits the Moon in an almost circular orbit at a height of $100\,\text{km}$ above the surface of the Moon. Look up the mass and the radius of the Moon in the MAFY table (mafytaulukot.fi). Calculate the probe's period of revolution. Give the answer in minutes.
hints: The values are found in the MAFY table under *Aurinkokunta* (the Solar System).

level2.text: A satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit at the speed $5.00\,\text{km/s}$. The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $6371\,\text{km}$. At what altitude above the surface does the satellite orbit? Give the answer in kilometres.

A probe orbiting Mars follows a circular orbit at an altitude of $400\,\text{km}$ above the surface of Mars. The mass of Mars is $6.42 \cdot 10^{23}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $3390\,\text{km}$. Calculate the orbital speed of the probe. Give the answer in kilometres per second.

At the surface of the Moon the acceleration of free fall is $1.62\,\text{m/s}^2$ and the radius of the Moon is $1737\,\text{km}$. What speed is needed for a probe to orbit the Moon in a circular orbit just above its surface? The Moon has no atmosphere. Give the answer in kilometres per second.

An astronaut of mass $75\,\text{kg}$ works on a space station at an altitude of $410\,\text{km}$. The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $6371\,\text{km}$. How large is the gravitational force acting on the astronaut, although the astronaut is weightless?

The table gives the orbital radius $r$ and the orbital period $T$ of the four largest moons of Jupiter (example data, rounded from the real values). The moons orbit Jupiter in nearly circular orbits.

The circular-orbit model gives $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\gamma M} r^3$, where $M$ is the mass of Jupiter. Calculate the ratio $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}$ for each moon in SI units and note that the ratio is almost the same.

Determine the mass of Jupiter from the mean of the ratios. Give the answer in the unit $10^{27}\,\text{kg}$.

level2.text:
The table gives the altitude above the surface $h$ and the orbital speed $v$ of four satellites orbiting the Earth (example data). The orbits are nearly circular. One of the speeds has been recorded in the table incorrectly.

The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $6371\,\text{km}$. Calculate the speed in a circular orbit for each satellite and find the incorrect value.

What is the correct value of the incorrect speed? Give the answer in kilometres per second.

data.caption: Altitude and orbital speed of the satellites

level2.text:
Two satellites, of masses $500\,\text{kg}$ and $2000\,\text{kg}$, are each placed in a circular orbit at an altitude of $800\,\text{km}$ above the surface of the Earth. A student reasons: “A fourfold gravitational force acts on the heavier satellite, so it orbits faster.”

The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $6371\,\text{km}$.

a) Calculate the gravitational force acting on each satellite.

b) Calculate the orbital speed of the heavier satellite.

c) Explain where the student's reasoning goes wrong.

The answer field takes the result of part b) in kilometres per second.

The right side of the figure shows the orbit of Halley's comet round the Sun. Read from the figure the comet's smallest and largest distance from the Sun. How many times greater would the orbital speed in a circular orbit be at the smallest distance than at the largest one, if a body went round the Sun in a circular orbit with that distance as its radius?

level3.text: Mars rotates once about its axis in $24\,\text{h}\;37\,\text{min}$. A communications satellite orbiting Mars is to stay all the time above the same point of the surface, like a geostationary satellite above the Earth. The mass of Mars is $6.42 \cdot 10^{23}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $3390\,\text{km}$. At what altitude above the surface of Mars must the satellite orbit? Give the answer in kilometres.

Thin air brakes a space station, and its nearly circular orbit descends over weeks from an altitude of $400\,\text{km}$ to an altitude of $398\,\text{km}$. The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $6371\,\text{km}$. Does the orbital speed of the station increase or decrease, and by how much? Give the change in the orbital speed in metres per second (an increase as positive). Do not round intermediate results before the subtraction.

The Earth rotates once about its axis in a day. How short would the rotation period of the Earth have to be for a person standing at the equator to be weightless? The mass of the Earth is $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$ and its radius $6371\,\text{km}$, and the shape of the Earth is assumed to be a sphere. Give the answer in minutes.

The table gives the orbital radius $r$ and the orbital period $T$ of four planets of a distant star (example data). The planets orbit the star in nearly circular orbits, and the mass of the star is much greater than the masses of the planets. The mass of the star is not known.

The circular-orbit model gives $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\gamma M} r^3$, where $M$ is the mass of the star. The orbital period of one planet has been measured incorrectly.

a) Calculate the ratio $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}$ for each planet in SI units. Deduce which planet's value is incorrect and justify why it is left out.

b) Determine the mass of the star from the mean of the ratios of the three other planets. Give the answer in the unit $10^{30}\,\text{kg}$.

c) Deduce what the orbital period of the incorrect planet should be and suggest what kind of measurement error could explain the deviation.

The answer field takes the result of part b).

data.caption: Orbital radius and orbital period of the planets of the star

level3.text:
Two satellites, A and B, orbit the Earth in the same plane and in the same direction in nearly circular orbits. The altitude of satellite A above the surface is $400\,\text{km}$ and that of satellite B $1000\,\text{km}$. Assume that the atmosphere does not brake the satellites and that their masses are much smaller than the mass of the Earth, $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$. The radius of the Earth is $6371\,\text{km}$.

At a certain moment the satellites are on the same straight line with the centre of the Earth and on the same side of the Earth.

a) Calculate the orbital period of each satellite.

b) How long does it take before the satellites are again on the same straight line with the centre of the Earth, on the same side, for the first time? Give the answer in hours. Do not round intermediate results.

c) The masses of the satellites were not given. Justify why they are not needed.

The answer field takes the result of part b).
